releases.title: Agent Team Starter Kit
releases.summary: A configurable generator and template set for scaffolding specialized AI agent roles around a visible GitHub Issues work queue and outcome gates.
releases.originalState: Complex work can arrive as an unstructured request with unclear ownership, hidden handoffs, and no durable record of what each specialist contributed.
releases.delivered: The public starter kit packages a Python generator, configurable persona and workflow templates, GitHub Issues and Actions patterns, and Azure Functions and Azure OpenAI integration scaffolding.
releases.outcome: The pattern is designed to make multi-agent work easier to assign, inspect, and govern while keeping the work item and its history visible to people.

valueEvidence.statement: Designed value: clearer ownership, inspectable handoffs, and human-visible outcome gates for multi-agent work.

capabilities: Generates configurable specialist persona and workflow files.
Uses GitHub Issues and Actions templates for a durable, visible work queue.
Provides scaffolding for Azure Functions and Azure OpenAI integration.
Includes outcome framing, validation, and human intervention patterns.

architecture.label: Issue
architecture.detail: A GitHub issue holds the request, context, and visible work state.

architecture.label: Workflow templates
architecture.detail: GitHub Actions and issue-handling templates describe routing and intervention points.

architecture.label: Generated personas
architecture.detail: Configurable specialist files scaffold bounded roles that deployers must complete and wire.

architecture.label: Human gate
architecture.detail: A person can inspect the work record and decide whether the outcome is acceptable.

guardrails: GitHub keeps the request, discussion, and resulting work visible rather than hiding them in a transient chat.
Specialist roles and outcome gates can be configured for the workflow instead of granting one agent an undefined remit.
People remain responsible for reviewing consequential outputs and deployment choices.
limitations: This is scaffolding rather than turnkey autonomy: generated personas include TODOs, the runner is a stub, and deployers must complete the domain logic and wiring.
Setup requires Python, authenticated GitHub CLI access, Azure Storage, Azure OpenAI, and secured repository permissions.
Evaluation, monitoring, cost controls, and domain-specific safety checks still need to be designed for each use.

provenance.label: Agent Team Starter Kit public repository
provenance.note: Public README, quick start, generator, workflow templates, and orchestrator source are the evidence base for this entry.

visual.alt: A GitHub issue moves through workflow templates and generated persona scaffolding to a human outcome gate.

article.title: Making multi-agent work visible
article.dek: A public starter kit uses GitHub Issues as the control surface for specialist agents, explicit handoffs, and human-reviewed outcomes.

releases.title: Customer 360 for Entities
releases.summary: An adaptive Dynamics 365 and Dataverse web resource that brings related operational context into the forms where work already happens.
releases.originalState: A person working in a business record can have to open multiple forms or related lists to assemble the cases, orders, entitlements, contacts, and other context needed for the next action.
releases.delivered: The public solution provides an adaptive JavaScript web resource for Dynamics 365 and Dataverse forms that retrieves and presents related entity context in one place.
releases.outcome: The design is intended to reduce context switching and make the surrounding record history easier to scan before a person chooses the next action.

valueEvidence.statement: Designed value: less navigation between related records and a more coherent operational view at the point of work.

capabilities: Embeds a reusable web resource in Dynamics 365 or Dataverse model-driven forms.
Presents related entity information such as cases, orders, entitlements, and contacts.
Adapts the view to the current record and available related data.
Keeps the user in the host business application while they review context.

architecture.label: Current record
architecture.detail: A model-driven form supplies the current entity and record context.

architecture.label: Web resource
architecture.detail: Client-side JavaScript initializes the adaptive experience.

architecture.label: Dataverse
architecture.detail: Approved queries retrieve related operational records.

architecture.label: User action
architecture.detail: The person reviews the unified context and remains responsible for the next action.

guardrails: The experience uses the host application's identity and Dataverse permissions rather than creating a separate authority boundary.
The component presents context; it does not replace the person's judgment or automatically commit consequential changes.
Deployers must limit queries and displayed fields to information users are already authorized to access.
limitations: The solution requires configuration for each Dataverse schema, form, and relationship set.
Performance depends on query design, related-record volume, and the host environment.
The public repository is a community solution and not a Microsoft-supported product.

provenance.label: Customer 360 for Entities public repository
provenance.note: Public README, deployment guidance, web-resource source, and solution files are the evidence base for this entry.

visual.alt: A model-driven form passes record context to a web resource, which retrieves related Dataverse data for user review.

article.title: Bring the surrounding record into the work
article.dek: An adaptive form component assembles related Dataverse context without turning context gathering into another application.

releases.title: Freight Triage Control Tower
releases.summary: A public sample-data browser prototype that models freight email triage as owned, visible work with queue, aging, detail, and resolution views.
releases.originalState: Exception signals can remain trapped in email and ad hoc follow-up, making ownership, age, priority, and resolution status difficult to see across an operations team.
releases.delivered: The public React and TypeScript Power Apps Code App packages control-tower lanes, owner assignment, email-thread context, SLA views, and resolution actions over fictional sample data persisted in browser localStorage.
releases.outcome: The design is intended to turn scattered exception signals into explicit work items with visible ownership and service-level context.

valueEvidence.statement: Designed value: a shared queue for freight exceptions with clearer ownership, aging, priority, and resolution state.

capabilities: Models freight email work as structured queue items over fictional sample data.
Shows queue, item detail, aging, and resolution views.
Supports explicit owner assignment, resolution, and reopening actions.
Calculates prototype SLA and aging metrics over the local sample records.

architecture.label: Sample email work
architecture.detail: Fictional shipment messages and threads supply the prototype queue.

architecture.label: Mock provider
architecture.detail: A shared data-provider interface persists mutable sample items and emails in browser localStorage.

architecture.label: Control tower
architecture.detail: Power Apps views expose queue, age, priority, detail, and status.

architecture.label: Owned resolution
architecture.detail: An operations user reviews assistance, takes action, and records the outcome.

guardrails: The prototype uses fictional carriers, shipment numbers, messages, and metrics rather than operational data.
Assignment, resolution, and reopening are explicit user actions.
A named operations owner remains accountable for the recorded resolution.
limitations: The current implementation uses a mock localStorage provider; Dataverse is described as a future provider swap, not a delivered integration.
Authentication, authorization, concurrency, audit, connectors, and production escalation policy are not implemented.
The repository does not establish measured operational improvement or production adoption.

provenance.label: Freight Triage Control Tower public repository
provenance.note: Public project README, data-provider interface, mock provider, state actions, and synthetic scenario content are the evidence base for this entry.

releases.title: Warranty + Claims Operations
releases.summary: A Power Platform accelerator for structuring warranty and claims intake, review, supporting flows, and human-owned decisions.
releases.originalState: Warranty and claims work can span inconsistent intake, supporting documents, policy checks, status questions, and handoffs that are difficult to trace as one case.
releases.delivered: The public accelerator packages Dataverse tables, Canvas Apps, Power Automate flows, and Copilot Studio agents as a starting point for warranty and claims operations.
releases.outcome: The design is intended to create a more consistent case record, guide information gathering, and keep approval or exception decisions with accountable people.

valueEvidence.statement: Designed value: more consistent claims intake and review with visible status, supporting context, and human-owned decisions.

capabilities: Defines Dataverse structures for warranty and claims workflow data.
Provides Canvas App experiences for intake and operations review.
Uses flows to coordinate repeatable process steps and notifications.
Demonstrates Copilot Studio agents for guided questions and assistance.

architecture.label: Claim intake
architecture.detail: A Canvas App or guided conversation captures the claim and supporting context.

architecture.label: Dataverse case
architecture.detail: Structured tables hold the case, evidence, status, and relationships.

architecture.label: Flows and agents
architecture.detail: Automation and Copilot Studio assistance support routing and information gathering.

architecture.label: Human decision
architecture.detail: An authorized reviewer remains responsible for approval, exception handling, and final disposition.

guardrails: Copilot Studio assistance does not replace policy, legal, financial, or approval authority.
Consequential claim decisions remain with authorized reviewers.
Deployers must configure security roles, data retention, audit, connector policy, and jurisdiction-specific requirements.
limitations: The accelerator is a starting point and requires tailoring to policy, product, region, and operating model.
The public repository does not establish measured savings, accuracy, or production performance.
Document verification, fraud controls, integrations, and exception policy require additional implementation.

provenance.label: Warranty + Claims Operations public repository
provenance.note: Public README, solution inventory, agent definitions, app assets, and flow guidance are the evidence base for this entry.

releases.title: Prompt Escape
releases.summary: A multiplayer prompt-engineering escape room that turns clearer instructions, constraints, iteration, and creativity into a playable team challenge.
releases.originalState: Prompting concepts can stay abstract when learners only read examples instead of working through a shared problem with constraints, feedback, and room to iterate.
releases.delivered: The public project delivers a TypeScript and Express escape-room game with solo, cooperative, and versus modes, deterministic prompt scoring, hints, and themed challenges.
releases.outcome: The experience is designed to make prompt quality discussable and memorable through practice, comparison, and team reflection.

valueEvidence.statement: Designed value: an experiential way for teams to practice clearer prompts, constraints, iteration, and collaborative problem solving.

capabilities: Packages prompt-engineering concepts as a multiplayer game.
Uses clues and constraints to reward clearer instructions and iteration.
Supports team play and discussion rather than an isolated tutorial.
Uses keyword, synonym, and heuristic scoring rather than an external AI evaluation API.

architecture.label: Team challenge
architecture.detail: Players enter a shared scenario with a goal, clues, and constraints.

architecture.label: Prompt attempt
architecture.detail: The team writes and refines instructions for the challenge.

architecture.label: Game response
architecture.detail: The application returns challenge feedback and progression state.

architecture.label: Team reflection
architecture.detail: Players compare approaches and decide how to improve the next attempt.

guardrails: The game is a learning experience, not a benchmark of a person or model.
Facilitators should avoid entering sensitive, personal, or proprietary information into prompts.
AI responses are part of the challenge and should be treated as fallible output.
limitations: The WorkIQ hint service currently returns mock responses rather than making live MCP calls.
The experience does not measure durable skill improvement or workplace outcomes.
The repository-listed hosted site returned HTTP 403 during verification, so current public hosting is not established.

provenance.label: Prompt Escape public repository
provenance.note: Public README, lobby manager, prompt evaluator, game engine, and WorkIQ service source are the evidence base for this entry.

visual.alt: A team challenge leads to a prompt attempt, game feedback, and team reflection before another iteration.

article.title: Teach prompting as a team sport
article.dek: A multiplayer escape room makes instructions, constraints, iteration, and reflection part of the learning loop.

releases.title: Copilot Studio + MCP Lab
releases.summary: A hands-on public lab for deploying a small Model Context Protocol tool server and adding it as a tool in Microsoft Copilot Studio.
releases.originalState: MCP concepts can be difficult to connect to practice when the protocol, server deployment, tool definition, client configuration, and invocation path are learned separately.
releases.delivered: The public lab uses a deliberately small TypeScript joke server to walk through MCP tools, Azure Container Apps deployment, a custom connector, and connection from Microsoft Copilot Studio.
releases.outcome: The lab is designed to give builders a bounded end-to-end reference they can inspect before adapting the pattern to a real tool.

valueEvidence.statement: Designed value: a compact end-to-end MCP reference that makes server, tool, client, and invocation responsibilities easier to see.

capabilities: Implements a small public MCP server and callable tool.
Documents deployment and connection steps for the lab.
Exposes four bounded tools backed by two public joke APIs.
Includes Azure Container Apps deployment infrastructure and Copilot Studio setup guidance.

architecture.label: Copilot client
architecture.detail: A user invokes the configured tool from Microsoft Copilot Studio.

architecture.label: MCP request
architecture.detail: The client sends a protocol request using the published tool contract.

architecture.label: Tool server
architecture.detail: The deployed sample server executes the bounded joke operation.

architecture.label: User response
architecture.detail: The client presents the tool result for the user to accept, ignore, or continue from.

guardrails: The sample tool is deliberately non-consequential and does not perform business writes.
The user chooses whether to invoke the tool and how to use its response.
The deployment guide warns that the lab creates a public MCP endpoint and recommends removing it after use.
Real tools require authentication, authorization, input validation, logging, and least-privilege design beyond the sample.
limitations: The lab demonstrates a narrow sample tool rather than a production MCP operating model, and no automated tests are configured.
Repository license metadata is inconsistent: GitHub detects MIT while the package manifest declares ISC.
The support file remains an unedited template, and the example does not establish security, reliability, or support guarantees.

provenance.label: Copilot Studio + MCP Lab public repository
provenance.note: Public README, MCP server source, Bicep deployment assets, package manifest, and support file are the evidence base for this entry.

visual.alt: A Copilot client sends an MCP request to a bounded tool server and presents the result back to the user.

article.title: Use a tiny tool to see the whole MCP path
article.dek: A deliberately small joke server makes the protocol boundary, deployment step, client connection, and user invocation easy to inspect.

releases.title: Home Assistant Estate Panel
releases.summary: A self-hosted React and TypeScript reference build that combines native Home Assistant cards with custom estate controls on a shared connection and layout.
releases.originalState: A self-hosted smart-home estate can accumulate separate dashboards, device views, and integration-specific controls that make routine status checks and actions harder to coordinate.
releases.delivered: The public repository implements a full-page Home Assistant panel and Lovelace custom card using React, TypeScript, selective websocket subscriptions, native and community card wrappers, invented sample configuration, and confirmation dialogs for security-reducing actions.
releases.outcome: The pattern is designed to create one adaptable local control surface while keeping real estate configuration outside the public repository and preserving deliberate review for sensitive actions.

valueEvidence.statement: Designed value: a coherent self-hosted estate view with selective live updates, reusable Home Assistant cards, and confirmation before security-reducing actions.

capabilities: Registers both a full-page Home Assistant panel and a Lovelace custom card.
Uses home-assistant-js-websocket with selective useSyncExternalStore subscriptions.
Wraps built-in and community Home Assistant cards alongside custom React components.
Separates invented sample configuration from git-ignored local household configuration.

architecture.label: Home Assistant
architecture.detail: An existing self-hosted Home Assistant environment provides entities, services, and the authenticated connection.

architecture.label: Selective store
architecture.detail: Websocket-backed external-store subscriptions update only the entity views that need new state.

architecture.label: React panel
architecture.detail: Custom components and wrapped Home Assistant cards share one estate layout.

architecture.label: Confirmed action
architecture.detail: Security-reducing operations require an explicit confirmation before a service call is sent.

guardrails: The committed sample estate is invented; real household configuration belongs in a git-ignored local file.
Security-reducing actions use confirmation dialogs before Home Assistant service calls.
The design remains self-hosted and does not claim to replace professional monitoring.
limitations: The card wrapper relies on window.loadCardHelpers(), which Home Assistant explicitly does not expose as a public API and may change.
An existing Home Assistant environment is required, and several community integrations are described as tinker-grade rather than supported dependencies.
The repository has no project LICENSE; dependency licenses do not grant reuse rights for the repository's original code.
No public evidence establishes reliability, security effectiveness, savings, adoption, or household outcomes.

provenance.label: Home Assistant Estate Panel public repository
provenance.note: Public application entry points, entity-store hooks, card wrapper, invented sample configuration, confirmation flow, README, package manifests, and history support this entry.

releases.title: Customer News Hub
releases.summary: An explicitly unpublished static reference interface for exploring how sample product updates could be filtered, scanned, and opened as a digest.
releases.originalState: People following product changes can face a long stream of announcements without an easy way to narrow the material by product, workload, category, persona, or a specific question.
releases.delivered: The public repository packages a static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript reference interface with embedded sample items, product and persona filters, card and digest views, a details dialog, escaped rendered values, and manifest/hash metadata.
releases.outcome: The design is intended to make a future public update digest easier to scan and tailor while keeping this build clearly separated from live announcements or an operating ingestion service.

valueEvidence.statement: Designed value: a filterable reference pattern for turning a broad product-update stream into a more focused, reviewable digest.

capabilities: Filters illustrative items by product, workload, category, persona, and free text.
Offers both card and digest reading views.
Uses a details dialog for deeper item context without leaving the interface.
Escapes rendered values and publishes manifest/hash metadata for the static sample package.

architecture.label: Demo digest
architecture.detail: Hand-authored illustrative records provide the only content source in the public repository.

architecture.label: Client filters
architecture.detail: Browser JavaScript applies product, workload, category, persona, and text filters.

architecture.label: Reading views
architecture.detail: Card and digest layouts present the filtered sample records.

architecture.label: User review
architecture.detail: A person opens details and follows any source link rather than relying on an automated action.

guardrails: The interface and manifest identify the experience as demo, illustrative, and unpublished.
Rendered data values are escaped before insertion into the interface.
The repository's robots file blocks indexing, and this journal does not link to the reachable but unapproved Pages build.
limitations: Every bundled item is hand-authored demo data rather than a live product announcement.
No live-source adapter, ingestion backend, or update process is implemented in the repository.
The repository manifest says publicState is false, the page labels itself unpublished, and robots.txt disallows indexing.
A bundled illustrative source link returned 404 during public verification, and the repository has no project LICENSE.

provenance.note: Public static source, embedded sample digest, filters, rendering code, manifest, robots policy, and repository history support this entry.

releases.title: SellerSphere Partner Accelerator
releases.summary: A sanitized, buildable reference accelerator for a voice-first Dynamics 365 seller experience with consumer-owned configuration and explicit approval gates.
releases.originalState: A field demonstration can be tightly coupled to one tenant, configured agent, data model, and preview feature set, which makes it unsafe and impractical to share as a reusable implementation reference.
releases.delivered: The public repository delivers sanitized desktop web-resource source, architecture, build and configuration guidance, an agent-instruction baseline, security controls, and sample workflows while excluding configured tenant artifacts and experimental bindings.
releases.outcome: The accelerator is designed to help a consumer build and govern its own voice-first Dynamics 365 reference experience without representing the package as a turnkey product or preapproved architecture.

valueEvidence.statement: Designed value: a safer starting point for consumer-owned voice, Copilot Studio, and Dynamics 365 integration with explicit approval before consequential actions.

capabilities: Hosts a desktop web resource inside a Dynamics 365 model-driven application.
Uses delegated MSAL authentication to reach a consumer-owned Copilot Studio agent and approved context.
Documents optional Azure AI Speech and Translator integration.
Separates proposed actions and draft communications from approved CRM writes or sends.

architecture.label: Seller web resource
architecture.detail: A desktop model-driven-app web resource captures the user request and optional speech input.

architecture.label: Delegated identity
architecture.detail: MSAL obtains delegated access for the consumer-owned agent and approved data context.

architecture.label: Proposed action
architecture.detail: Copilot Studio and approved tools assemble a proposed CRM action or draft communication.

architecture.label: Explicit approval
architecture.detail: The user approves a CRM update and separately authorizes any communication send.

guardrails: Agent instructions limit execution to approved tools and prohibit guessed CRM identifiers.
CRM writes require explicit approval, communications remain drafts by default, and sending requires separate authorization.
Ambiguous requests require clarification rather than silent assumptions.
limitations: This is source-level reference material, not a production app, managed solution, supported Microsoft offering, one-click deployment, or preapproved governance design.
Consumers must build, configure, secure, test, and govern their own deployment; mobile authentication is disabled.
The web resource can retain up to five conversations with business context in browser localStorage, requiring explicit privacy, retention, shared-device, and clearing controls.
The repository-declared Pages site is a release and terms landing page, not the authenticated application.

releases.title: Deal to Glory
releases.summary: A single-commit hackathon MVP that visualizes a deterministic, agent-styled seller workflow from voice or text input through CRM, illustrative attainment, recognition, and simulated notification stages.
releases.originalState: A spoken seller update may need to be translated into structured CRM intent, an opportunity action, an illustrative attainment view, recognition language, and a communication payload across separate steps.
releases.delivered: The public MVP implements a sequential TypeScript pipeline with keyword-based intent extraction, a mock or configured Dataverse opportunity stage, illustrative commission and attainment calculation, recognition copy, simulated notification output, Express Server-Sent Events, and browser speech or text input.
releases.outcome: The prototype is designed to make a multi-stage seller workflow visible as one narrated sequence, not to establish autonomous AI behavior, production safety, or measured seller impact.

valueEvidence.statement: Designed value: a tangible visualization of how one seller update could pass through structured CRM, calculation, recognition, and notification stages.

capabilities: Accepts browser Web Speech or text input and streams stage progress with Server-Sent Events.
Uses deterministic keyword extraction rather than an external AI model for deal intent.
Runs a mock path or an optional configured Dataverse opportunity update.
Produces illustrative attainment, recognition, and simulated notification payloads.

architecture.label: Voice or text
architecture.detail: The browser captures a seller update through Web Speech or typed input.

architecture.label: Deterministic stages
architecture.detail: Sequential TypeScript stages extract intent and compose the workflow.

architecture.label: CRM and calculation
architecture.detail: A mock or configured Dataverse action is followed by illustrative attainment logic.

architecture.label: Simulated notice
architecture.detail: Recognition and notification payloads are composed, but the Teams-style send is simulated.

guardrails: The journal labels the stages deterministic and agent-styled rather than claiming five autonomous AI agents.
Attainment and commission values are illustrative rather than financial evidence.
A real Dataverse deployment should add an explicit approval gate before any mutation; the current optional write path does not provide one.
limitations: When Dataverse is configured, speech completion starts the pipeline and the opportunity stage can write without an explicit user approval gate.
The notification endpoint logs intent and returns success without sending a real Teams message, while the payload marks the channel simulated.
The server enables unrestricted CORS with no authentication middleware, and browser what-if values are inserted through innerHTML without escaping.
Date handling is hard-coded around 2026, and the repository has no LICENSE file even though package.json says MIT.

provenance.label: Deal to Glory public repository
provenance.note: Public orchestrator, voice-intake, opportunity, notification, server, browser, package metadata, README, and single-commit history support this entry.

attribution.relationship: Upstream Azure identity dependency used by the optional Dataverse path.

article.dek: Deal to Glory makes a five-stage workflow visible while its source reveals the important limits: deterministic extraction, illustrative calculations, simulated notification, and an ungated optional CRM write path.
